epic.summary: Data Platform Foundation: one trusted, cheap, boring platform for everything that follows
epic.description:
**Sponsor:** Sam Okafor, Director of IT.

> "Every department runs on its own exports. Marcus pulls a WMS CSV for Ops every Monday by hand, Finance rebuilds
> the same numbers from AX in Excel every month-end, and Sales Ops keeps a third client list in Salesforce.
> Nobody can tell me how many active clients we have." (Sam)

Daniel Reyes has told the board that Harborline will have a single, trusted data platform by year-end. Three
departments (Operations, Finance, Transportation) are queued behind it. This project is the foundation everything
after it stands on, so Sam would rather it be boring and solid than clever.

**How this project runs:** the first sprint is small, concrete steps (a first connection, a first table, a first
number, a first pull request). The second sprint adds what keeps it running without you.

**What this project delivers**
- Your engineering setup and repository standards, so anyone who joins later works the same way.
- A cloud data platform with separate dev and prod, secrets handled properly, and costs inside the free tier.
- The WMS landed every day, starting with one table, and a first silver layer on top of it.
- Every insert, update and delete captured, plus history the WMS itself throws away.
- A data-quality framework that quarantines bad rows instead of hiding them.
- Scheduled, retried, alerting pipelines, and CI on every pull request.
- Dashboard **P1-D1 Data Platform Health**: can yesterday's data be trusted?

**Constraints**
- Sources are on-prem (your machine, behind Harborline's firewall). Kevin O'Hara will not open inbound ports.
- Free tier first. Sam wants to hear about a paid limit before it is hit, not after.
- Dataset: on Large about 3 years, ~2.5 M orders, ~7 M order lines and ~20 M inventory-ledger rows (Medium is 2 years and about 40% of that), plus a continuous
  stream of inserts, updates and deletes when the simulator is running.

**Success measures**
- Five consecutive scheduled runs land everything the WMS changed since the previous run, with no manual steps.
- Every data-quality failure is recorded and visible on P1-D1.
- Release **v0.1.0** tagged on `main` with a CHANGELOG and the ADRs that explain the platform.

**Out of scope:** Finance, CRM and carrier pipelines (Projects 3-5), streaming CDC (Project 6).

stories.summary: Workstation, first connection and first pull request
stories.description:
Before anyone writes a pipeline, Sam wants the basics right: a working machine, a first query against the WMS, and
a repository that enforces how the team works.

> "The last contractor's scripts lived on a laptop with passwords in them. When he left, so did the pipelines.
> That doesn't happen again." (Sam)

The tickets here are small and in order. Do them one at a time, top to bottom.

**Why now:** every later ticket assumes a branch per ticket, Conventional Commits with the ticket key, a PR with
self-review and pre-commit secret scanning. Adding standards later costs ten times more.

**Talk to:** Kevin O'Hara (machine, Docker, network) and Mei Tanaka (what counts as a secret and what must never be committed).

**Where to start:** The **Getting Started** handbook page has the install steps, then take P1.S1.T1.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done; your repository is on GitHub with `main` protected
- At least one PR merged through the full flow: branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…` → Conventional Commits with the key → PR template → self-review → merge
- The ADR template and CHANGELOG.md exist on `main`; the source inventory is linked from the README
acceptance_criteria: The simulator runs on your machine with a Medium or Large build finished; the Control Center is reachable at http://localhost:8080
You can query wms, ax2012 and iot as etl_reader and call the mock Salesforce and carrier APIs
Your own GitHub repository exists with a protected main (PR required, no force-push, no deletion)
PR template, issue templates, CODEOWNERS and pre-commit (gitleaks, ruff, sqlfluff) are committed
A planted fake secret is blocked by pre-commit before it reaches a commit
A source inventory covers every Harborline source system

tasks.summary: Set up the workstation with the setup file
tasks.description:
Run the setup file (SETUP-WINDOWS.cmd or SETUP-MAC.command) until it finishes with ALL DONE. It installs what's
missing and skips the rest. If it stops, paste its report to Kevin O'Hara, do what he says and run it again.
Note anything that went wrong or took longer than expected; Sam wants that feedback so the next hire's setup
is faster.

**Where to start:** Run the file from the folder you downloaded; Getting Started → *Run the setup file* says what each step does.
acceptance_criteria: The setup file finishes with ALL DONE
Docker Desktop has at least the memory the handbook recommends
Git identity and SSH key work against GitHub; gh auth status is clean
Setup notes (time spent, gotchas) saved, to be committed once the repository exists

tasks.summary: Build the dataset and run your first query
tasks.description:
Start the simulator and run a Medium or Large build, if setup has not done it already (Medium is 2 years of history, Large 3; the Control Center shows an estimate).
On the first-release path, Small is enough. Rebuild at Medium before you go further: a rebuild leaves your tickets alone.

Then make your first connection: Postgres, database `wms`, as `etl_reader`, the same login your pipelines will use.
Run one query and look at the result. Don't build anything yet.

Finally, press **Generate batch** once in the Control Center and run the query again, so you see the source change
underneath you.

**Where to start:** Getting Started → *Try each source system* has the connection details and the query. Open it
from the `Harborline WMS` connection in DBeaver. Stuck? Kevin O'Hara.
acceptance_criteria: Build completed; size, build time and row counts per system recorded
DBeaver connected as etl_reader to the wms database
The first query in Getting Started returns one row per warehouse, with its time zone
After one Generate batch you can say how many orders were added

tasks.summary: Finish your data repository and project skeleton
tasks.description:
The setup file created `harborline-analytics` on your machine and on your GitHub account, with a starter
README. The layout from here is your call, but someone new should understand it from the README in five
minutes. The simulator is not part of this repo.

CI will run on Linux, so line endings matter: read the `.gitattributes` it started you with.

**Where to start:** `harborline-analytics` on your machine. Open its README first. Ask Nadia Petrov if you can't decide on a folder name.

README states purpose, layout, how to run, and links to this epic
.gitignore keeps .env files, local data and credentials out; .gitattributes normalizes line endings
Your first commit on the skeleton follows Conventional Commits and carries this ticket's key
Setup notes from P1.S1.T1 committed under docs/

tasks.summary: Your first pull request: protect main and add templates
tasks.description:
Sam's rule: nothing reaches `main` without a pull request, and every PR tells a reviewer what changed, why, how
it was tested and what could break. You're the only engineer building this, so the first reviewer is you tomorrow
morning; Nadia Petrov will look when you ask. The self-review checklist is not optional.

The setup file started this: a ruleset on `main`, a PR template and a bug template. Check them against the
criteria below and finish what's missing. Keep the change small: the point is to learn the full flow.

**Where to start:** Getting Started → *Your own repository* has every command. The project brief's *Git and
engineering standards* says why.
acceptance_criteria: Branch protection or a ruleset on main requires a PR, blocks force-pushes and deletion
PR template covers summary, ticket link, testing evidence, data impact, rollback and a self-review checklist
Issue templates exist for bug, data request and spike
CODEOWNERS committed
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Pre-commit hooks for secrets, Python and SQL
tasks.description:
The setup file installed pre-commit with gitleaks (secrets), ruff (Python lint and format) and sqlfluff (SQL
lint). Prove it works. sqlfluff has a provisional dialect: revisit it after the platform decision (P1.S2.T1).

Mei Tanaka's standard: a secret that reaches a remote is a security incident, even in a private repository.
The same hooks will run in CI later (P1.S5), so nobody can skip them with `--no-verify`.

**Where to start:** Run `pre-commit run --all-files` in your repository, then try committing a scratch file with a made-up key in it.
Ask Mei Tanaka what she counts as a secret.
acceptance_criteria: pre-commit config committed with gitleaks, ruff and sqlfluff; hook versions pinned
Hooks run on every commit on your machine
A fake credential in a scratch file is blocked; the test is described in the PR, not committed
README explains how to install the hooks
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Conventional Commits, CHANGELOG and release policy
tasks.description:
Every project in this program ends with a release tag. Write down how versions are bumped and how the CHANGELOG is

**Where to start:** Copy the rules from the project brief's *Commit messages* and *Releases, CHANGELOG and ADRs*

Release policy written down: one tag per project, v0.1.0 at the end of this project
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
> "Our last platform migration failed partly because nobody remembered why things were built the way they were." (Sam)

Set up a lightweight Architecture Decision Record practice: a template and an index. You don't need to decide

tasks.description:

inventory a new engineer could use: what each system is, who owns it, how to connect, the tables or objects that

- **Marcus Bell**: WMS (housekeeping jobs, how timestamps and deletes behave)

- **Dana Whitfield**: Salesforce
- **Tomás Ortega**: EDI and the carrier tracking feed

Inventory covers WMS, AX 2012, IoT, Salesforce, carrier API, EDI and the landing files
Every WMS table listed with row count, primary key, change-tracking column (or none) and delete behaviour
Cross-system keys identified (client, tracking number, client PO, worker) with known quality concerns
Open questions listed with whom you asked and what they said

stories.summary: Cloud platform and environments
stories.description:
Harborline needs a home for its data. Sam has no budget for a paid platform this year, so start from a free tier:
**Databricks Free Edition** or a **Snowflake trial**. The trial ends after 30 days, so plan for day 31. Pick one,
justify it, and set it up with separate dev and prod and no shared passwords. Keep a list of what you create; it
goes into code in P1.S5.

**Constraints**
- Free-tier limits are real. Databricks Free Edition is serverless-only, with one small SQL warehouse, a cap on
  concurrent job tasks and daily usage quotas. A Snowflake trial has a credit cap and an end date. Know the limits
  and design within them.
- The sources are on-prem, and Kevin O'Hara won't open inbound firewall ports, so the cloud cannot pull from
  Postgres directly.
- Mei Tanaka owns security policy. Ask her what she expects for secrets, access and consumer PII: ship-to names,
  addresses, phone numbers and e-mail addresses live in the WMS.

**Why now:** every later story deploys into this.

**Where to start:** Getting Started → *Your cloud platform*, then P1.S2.T1.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done; ADRs for platform and connectivity accepted and merged
- gitleaks is clean on the full git history
- Each sub-task merged through its own PR (branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…`, Conventional Commits with the key, self-review, checks green)
acceptance_criteria: Platform chosen in an accepted ADR comparing at least two options on cost, limits, features needed through Project 8, and exit plan
Separate dev and prod environments with documented naming conventions and access
Secrets live in a secret store or untracked local config, never in the repository
Cost guardrails configured and documented, including what happens when a free-tier quota is hit
The path from on-prem sources to the cloud is documented and respects the no-inbound-ports rule

tasks.summary: Spike: Databricks Free Edition vs Snowflake trial
tasks.description:
Time-box: 4 hours. Compare the options for Harborline's whole roadmap, not just this month. Later projects need
API ingestion, near-real-time CDC (Project 6, five-minute freshness), row-level security and PII masking
(Project 8) and dashboards. Include what breaks when the trial or quota runs out, and how you'd move off the platform.

Sam doesn't care which one you pick. He cares that you can defend it.

**Where to start:** Answer the questions in Getting Started → *Decide, with reasons*, one row per option. That table is most of the ADR.
acceptance_criteria: ADR-0001 (platform choice) with options, criteria, decision and consequences
Free-tier limits that affect the design listed, with links to the official documentation
Decision names the dashboard tool you'll use (platform-native, Power BI Desktop or Streamlit) and why
Time spent logged; no more than the time-box
Committed via PR (docs/DATA-<n>-… branch, Conventional Commit with the key) and linked from this ticket

tasks.description:
Create the account or workspace and the structures for two environments. You must be able to break dev with
no risk to prod, and prod should change only through a merged PR (fully enforced once CD exists in P1.S5).
Anyone reading an object name should know its environment and its layer (bronze, silver or gold).

Creating these by hand is fine for now, as long as you write down what you made. They go into code in P1.S5.T8.

On the first-release path, skip the spike for now and pick Databricks Free Edition, unless you have a reason not to.
You'll still write the comparison later, and it can change your mind.

**Where to start:** The project brief's *Environments and infrastructure*, then your platform's own quick-start.
acceptance_criteria: dev and prod separated (catalogs, databases or schemas; your design, documented)
Naming conventions for environments, layers, objects and service identities written down
A non-personal identity (service principal or service user) runs pipelines, separate from your login
Your personal login cannot write to prod outside the deployment path, or the free-tier gap is documented
A list of every object you created by hand is committed
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
Pipelines need the Postgres `etl_reader` password, the Salesforce client secret, the carrier API key and, if you take
Project 4's stretch comparison, an EIA API key. Decide where secrets live on your machine and on the platform, how code reads them, and how
you'd rotate one. Check Mei Tanaka's expectations first. She is strict and she will ask.

**Where to start:** Start with one secret, the `etl_reader` password: put it in `.env` (already ignored) and read it from code. The
project brief's *Secrets and personal data* has the rules; your platform's docs have its secret store.
acceptance_criteria: No secret in code, notebooks, config or git history (gitleaks run on the full history)
Local secrets kept in an untracked file or the OS credential store, documented in the README
Platform-side secrets kept in the platform's secret mechanism
Rotation drill done for one secret you control and written up in docs/runbook.md (start the file now; P1.S5.T7 finishes it)
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Decide how on-prem data reaches the cloud
tasks.description:
The sources sit on-prem: Postgres in Docker, a folder of landing files and two APIs. Kevin O'Hara's rule is no
inbound ports from the internet, so the cloud platform can't connect to Postgres directly. Decide how data
leaves the building, what runs where, what crosses the wire and how it's protected in transit.

Kevin and Mei both want to read this one.
acceptance_criteria: ADR (connectivity and data movement) accepted, with a simple diagram
States what runs on-prem and what runs in the cloud, and how each source's data moves
Covers encryption in transit and where each credential is used
Lists the consumer-PII columns that would leave the building and records Mei Tanaka's answer on how to handle them
Committed via PR (docs/DATA-<n>-… branch, Conventional Commit with the key) and linked from this ticket

tasks.summary: Cost guardrails for the free tier
tasks.description:
> "Keep it cheap, and never surprise me." (Sam)

Find out what costs money or consumes quota on your platform. Put guardrails in place: auto-stop or suspend,
small compute sizes, quotas or resource monitors, and budget alerts where the platform allows them. Document
what happens when a limit is hit, including how long you're blocked. These numbers feed the cost panel on P1-D1.

**Where to start:** Your platform's docs page on auto-stop or auto-suspend, then its page on quotas or resource monitors. The free-tier
limits you listed in P1.S2.T1 are the checklist.
acceptance_criteria: Every compute resource auto-stops or suspends within minutes of going idle
A budget or quota alert, resource monitor or documented free-tier equivalent exists
Free-tier quotas and what happens when each is exceeded documented in docs/runbook.md
Baseline usage for one day of development recorded
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

stories.summary: First WMS tables: a landed table, a first number, then every table and a first silver layer
stories.description:
Time to put real data in the platform, one small step at a time. Land the smallest WMS table, then see a number you
can check against the source. Then widen: every WMS table, a daily incremental load and a first silver layer, so
no department has to touch raw bronze data.

Marcus Bell can't change the WMS schema, and IT won't add triggers to it. The WMS has harder habits too: `order_line`
has no audit timestamp, rows are physically deleted and a nightly job purges old tasks. Those wait for P1.S4. Note
them, but don't solve them here.

**Constraints**
- Read-only access as `etl_reader`. For now Sam wants reliable batch loads; streaming CDC is planned for Project 6.
- The WMS is a production system in the daytime, so keep the extract load modest.
- Volume on Large: ~2.5 M orders, ~7 M lines and ~20 M `inventory_txn` rows over 3 years (Medium is about 40% of that over 2 years).

**Where to start:** P1.S3.T1, one table, and the connectivity ADR you just wrote.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done; the ingestion-strategy and modeling-tool ADRs are accepted
- All 28 WMS tables land in bronze with load metadata; the full backfill is complete
- Silver models for the WMS have tests
- Each sub-task merged through its own PR (branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…`, Conventional Commits with the key, self-review, checks green)
acceptance_criteria: A first table and a first number in the platform, checked against the source
Every WMS table lands in bronze with batch id, extract window and source row counts
Each table has a documented load strategy (full, incremental, append-only or snapshot comparison) and the reason
Tables with mod_ts load incrementally; re-running a load creates no duplicates
Full backfill completed within free-tier limits, with its duration documented
Layer conventions (bronze, silver, gold) documented: what each guarantees and who may read it
Silver WMS models are typed, one current row per business key, with UTC and local timestamps and canonical units

tasks.description:
Copy one table from the WMS to your dev environment, by the route your connectivity ADR describes (on the first-release path that ADR comes later, so a script on your machine is the route for now). `warehouse` is
the right first table: one row per site, no consumer data, nothing to get wrong. Copy the whole table, every time.
Don't build a framework yet. A short script is fine.

**Where to start:** Run `SELECT * FROM wms.warehouse` in DBeaver and note the row count. Write the script that lands
those rows in dev bronze, reading the password from where you put it in P1.S2.T3. Stuck? Nadia Petrov.
acceptance_criteria: wms.warehouse is in dev bronze with every source column and a load timestamp
Row count in the platform equals the row count in the WMS
Running the script twice leaves the same rows, not double
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Your first number: orders per site
tasks.description:
Sam's first question of any platform is whether its numbers are right. Land `order_header` in dev bronze, leaving out
every `ship_to_*` column, and join it to the `warehouse` table you landed. Show one number per site, orders received
in the last 30 days, in the dashboard tool you named in ADR-0001 (a saved query with a simple chart counts; on the first-release path, use your platform's own). Then
check it against the source.

**Where to start:** The first query in Getting Started → *Try each source system* is nearly this one. Run it in
DBeaver with a date filter, stop the stream so the source holds still, and keep that result to compare against.
acceptance_criteria: Orders received per site, last 30 days, shown in your dashboard tool
Every site's number equals the same query run against the WMS
No ship_to column in the platform; a screenshot with both results is in the PR
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Add tables by configuration: a config-driven extract
tasks.description:
Your first script copied one table. Turn it into something that copies any table, so adding a table is a line of
configuration, not code. Every batch must be traceable: which run produced it, when, how many rows the source had
and how many arrived. Full copies are fine for now.

**Where to start:** A YAML file in the repository with one entry per table (name, schema, load mode) and your P1.S3.T1
script reading it. Get `warehouse` and `owner` working before adding more.
acceptance_criteria: Tables and their load mode driven by configuration in the repository
Each batch carries run id, extract window and row counts and lands in bronze unchanged (append-only)
Source and landed row counts reconciled per table per run; a mismatch fails the run
Extract time for one day of full volume documented
Credentials read from the secret mechanism set up in P1.S2.T3
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
Run the initial full load of the full dataset into prod, and a smaller slice into dev. Watch the free-tier
limits: a careless backfill can burn a day's quota or a big share of the trial credits. Record how long it took
and what it consumed. Sam will ask.

**Where to start:** List your tables by size first (your inventory has the counts) and load small to large, so a mistake is cheap. Note
your quota before and after.
acceptance_criteria: Full backfill in prod; source and landed counts reconciled for every table
Duration, data volume and compute or credits used recorded in the runbook
dev holds a documented subset that is enough for development and CI
A failed backfill restarts from where it stopped
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
You've now seen every WMS table in your own platform. For each one, decide how you'll detect new, changed and deleted
rows, how often, and at what extract cost. The next tickets and P1.S4 implement this. Use what you learned in
discovery. Ask Marcus Bell anything you're unsure of: whether `mod_ts` is always set on update, when housekeeping
runs, which tables are append-only.
acceptance_criteria: Per-table matrix: grain, primary key, change signal, delete behaviour, strategy, frequency, expected daily volume
ADR (ingestion strategy) accepted, including why not streaming CDC yet
Edge cases listed: local-time watermarks across DST, late-committing transactions, warehouses in different time zones
Committed via PR (docs/DATA-<n>-… branch, Conventional Commit with the key) and linked from this ticket

tasks.summary: Incremental loads for tables with audit timestamps
tasks.description:
Most WMS tables carry `mod_ts`, which is local warehouse time and set by the application. Load only what changed
since the last successful run, without re-reading the world every time. Watermarks must survive restarts and failed
runs.

**Where to start:** One table, `owner`. Keep the highest `mod_ts` you loaded, per table, and next time read a little
before it (an overlap window) so late-committing rows aren't missed, then drop what you've already seen.
acceptance_criteria: Watermark state persisted per table and advanced only after a successful load
No missed updates when a simulator batch and an extract overlap in time (tested)
Behaviour across a DST change documented
Re-running the same window creates no duplicates
A column added by a WMS release (see sys_release) doesn't break the load and is reported
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.summary: Daily snapshots of AX customers and Salesforce accounts for the client crosswalk
tasks.description:
Every later project joins clients across three systems: WMS `owner.owner_code`, AX `custtable.accountnum` (the
name lives in `dirpartytable`) and the Salesforce `Account` (`WMS_Owner_Code__c`, `ERP_Account_Number__c`).
The full AX and Salesforce pipelines come in Project 3. For now, land a small daily snapshot of just these
customer and account records so the platform can check the crosswalk (P1.S4.T6).

Dana Whitfield can tell you about Salesforce API limits; Priya Raman about AX customers in the three legal entities.

**Where to start:** Getting Started → *Try each source system* has both the AX customer query and the Salesforce token and SOQL call.
Point them at bronze, once a day, as a new dated snapshot each time.
acceptance_criteria: Daily full snapshot of AX customers (all three legal entities, with party names) and Salesforce Accounts in bronze
Salesforce access uses OAuth client credentials and follows pagination to the end
Snapshot history kept so day-to-day changes can be compared
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
Choose the modeling tool (dbt Core, platform-native SQL or pipelines, or something else) and decide how bronze,
silver and gold are laid out, named and tested. Remember the free-tier limits, and that every later project
inherits this choice.

**Where to start:** If you have no reason to choose otherwise, dbt Core is a safe default. Read the project brief's *Environments and
infrastructure*, then write the ADR. Nadia Petrov reviews it.
acceptance_criteria: ADR (modeling tool and layers) accepted
Naming, materialization and testing conventions documented
Repository structure matches the ADR
Committed via PR (docs/DATA-<n>-… branch, Conventional Commit with the key) and linked from this ticket

tasks.summary: First silver models for the WMS
tasks.description:
Build silver for every WMS table Ops and Finance will use: one current row per business key, types enforced. All WMS
times are local to the row's warehouse (`warehouse.time_zone`), and downstream needs both UTC and local. Child tables
with no warehouse column still need a time zone.

Deleted rows come in P1.S4, so leave room for a deleted flag and a detected-at time.
acceptance_criteria: Silver models for all WMS tables, with primary-key uniqueness and not-null tests
Every timestamp available in UTC and local time, correct across DST transitions (tested on a fall-back night)
Incremental where it pays off; full rebuild time documented
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

tasks.description:
US sites record weights and dimensions in LB and IN; TOR1 and MTY1 use KG and CM. The unit is stored per row
(`weight_uom`, `dim_uom`), and some rows are wrong. Finance and Transportation will add weights across sites,
so silver must offer canonical units without losing the original values.

**Where to start:** `wms.material`, and a `GROUP BY` of its units per site, to see what's there.
acceptance_criteria: Canonical weight and dimension columns sit alongside the source values and units
Rows whose unit is implausible for their site or magnitude are flagged, ready to become a rule in P1.S4.T5
Canonical unit choice documented
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

stories.summary: Every change captured, and data quality you can see
stories.description:
The first sprint landed what the WMS shows today. Now capture what it hides.

**What makes the WMS hard** (from your inventory and Marcus Bell)
- `order_line` has no audit timestamp at all.
- Rows are physically deleted: inventory at zero quantity, cancelled order lines, abandoned draft orders, voided
  labels (`shipment_carton`), `billing_record` corrections before invoicing, ASNs cancelled before arrival, SKUs
  created in error.
- A nightly housekeeping job deletes `task` rows older than 180 days. Ops will want labor history older than that.

Just as important: when data is wrong, Sam wants to **see** it, not have it silently dropped or silently passed
through. The simulator injects realistic defects (orphans, duplicates, negative quantities, sentinel dates, unit
mix-ups, whitespace in keys, mojibake and more) at about 1 in 10,000 records per category by default. Your
framework should catch them, quarantine what's unusable and record every result.

**Why now:** Project 2 (Operations) builds on silver in two weeks.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done
- Inserts, updates and deletes from a simulator batch are reflected after the next load, proven by a reconciliation
- The DQ results table is populated on every run
- DQ precision and recall measured once against the simulator's answer key, recorded in the PR
- Each sub-task merged through its own PR (branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…`, Conventional Commits with the key, self-review, checks green)
acceptance_criteria: Updates are captured for order_line, including quantity changes
Hard deletes are detected for every table that deletes, with the time the deletion was detected
Task history older than 180 days survives the purge, and purges are distinguishable from cancellations
DQ rules declared as configuration with severity; every run records rule, table, rows checked, rows failed and sample keys
Rows failing error-level rules are quarantined with a reason and excluded from silver; warnings pass with a flag
Quarantined rows can be re-processed after a fix without a full reload
Cross-system client key match rate measured daily
DQ precision and recall measured against the simulator answer key

tasks.summary: Detect hard deletes, and keep task history beyond the 180-day purge
tasks.description:

`order_line` (cancelled), `shipment_carton` (voided labels), `billing_record` (pre-invoice corrections),
`asn_header` and `asn_line` (cancelled before arrival), `material` (SKUs created in error) and `task` (purge). The
list may not be complete; Marcus Bell would know. Downstream needs to know a row is gone, and when you noticed.

`task` needs extra care. The WMS deletes rows older than 180 days every night, and Luis Moreno's team will want labor
productivity history in Project 2. Keep tasks after the WMS forgets them, and never mistake a purge for a
cancellation. Ask Marcus when the purge runs and exactly what it removes.
acceptance_criteria: Every deleting table has delete detection; deleted rows are flagged in bronze and silver, not removed, with a detected-at time
Delete counts per table per run are recorded (they appear on P1-D1)
Detected deletes reconcile with the simulator's delete counts per table after a batch
Rows missing because of a partial or failed extract can never be recorded as deletes
Purged tasks remain in your history with their final state, classified separately from operational deletes
Documented how much task history existed at your first load, and what is lost for good
Merged via PR from a feat/DATA-<n>-… branch; Conventional Commits carry the key; PR self-review done; checks green

stories.summary: Orchestration and CI/CD
stories.description:
> "Right now the pipeline runs when you run it. I need it to run when nobody's watching, recover by itself when
> something blips, and tell IT when it can't." (Sam)

Sam also needs every change checked before it reaches prod, and everything you created by hand back in code.

**Requirements from IT**
- A scheduled daily run end to end (extract → bronze → silver → DQ), plus an on-demand run.
- Transient failures (network, API throttling, warehouse resume) retry. Real failures alert.
- Alerts go to IT (Sam and Kevin O'Hara); agree the channel with Kevin. An alert says what failed, where, and what to do next.
- A missed run (laptop off overnight or over a weekend) catches up by itself.
- CI on every pull request: lint, tests and a model build against dev. CD: a merge to `main` deploys to prod.

**Constraints:** the free tier caps concurrent tasks and compute, so the schedule and parallelism must respect that.
Part of the pipeline runs on-prem and part in the cloud, and orchestration has to cover both.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done; the orchestration and infrastructure-as-code ADRs are accepted
- Five consecutive scheduled runs succeeded with no manual steps (run history linked)
- dev and prod are reproducible from the repository; dev has been torn down and recreated from code once
- The runbook covers rerun, backfill, catch-up and alert response
- Each sub-task merged through its own PR (branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…`, Conventional Commits with the key, self-review, CI green)
acceptance_criteria: Daily schedule and on-demand trigger for the end-to-end pipeline, with task dependencies
Transient failures retried with backoff; re-running a step creates no duplicates
Missed runs caught up automatically, in order
Alerts on failure, freshness breach and error-level DQ failures reach the channel agreed with Kevin O'Hara
CI runs on every PR (lint, unit tests, model build and tests against dev) and is required by branch protection
A merge to main deploys to prod without manual steps; deployments are versioned
Environment objects are created from code in the repository, not by hand
Runbook in the repository

epic.summary: Warehouse Performance Scorecard: one set of Ops numbers every GM trusts
epic.description:
**Sponsor:** Luis Moreno, VP Operations. **Site partner:** Shanice Carter, GM ATL1.

> "I run eight buildings and every Monday I get eight spreadsheets that measure on-time eight different ways. When a
> client asks for OTIF in a quarterly review, my GMs scramble for two days and the answer still depends on who built
> the spreadsheet." (Luis)

Peak season (15 November to 24 December) is coming. Luis needs to know which sites are struggling *before* the
client calls him, and his GMs need to trust the numbers, which means they need to drill into their own building.

**What this project delivers**
- Reference data that makes measurement fair: site master, holidays, weather and a business-day calendar per site.
- Order, shipment, inventory and labor models built on the Project 1 silver layer.
- One agreed, owned definition for every scorecard KPI, computed in exactly one place.
- Dashboards **P2-D1 Warehouse Ops Scorecard** (network view) and **P2-D2 Site Operations Detail** (for GMs).

**KPIs Luis cares about:** OTIF, order cycle time, dock-to-stock, pick productivity, inventory accuracy and space
utilization. Fair warning from Luis: Client Success and Finance have their own ideas about what on-time means.

**Context**
- Eight sites in three countries. TOR1 and MTY1 work in kilograms and centimetres. CHI1 is cold chain and runs three
  shifts. LAX1 opened about a year and a half ago.
- All WMS times are local to the warehouse. US, Canadian and Mexican holidays differ.
- Volume on Large: ~2.5 M orders and ~7 M lines over 3 years (Medium is about 40% of that over 2 years); some verticals run at 3-4× normal volume in peak weeks.

**Success measures**
- The Monday ops call runs off P2-D1 instead of spreadsheets.
- Every GM confirms their site's numbers, and every KPI has a named owner who signed off its definition.
- Release **v0.2.0** tagged with CHANGELOG.

**Platform note:** if you're on the Snowflake path, your 30-day trial ends during this project. Re-provisioning from
the infrastructure code you wrote in P1.S5.T8 should be a non-event; if it isn't, fix that first.

stories.summary: Reference enrichment: site master, holidays, weather and business-day calendar
stories.description:
Raw WMS events don't know that Canadian Thanksgiving isn't the US one, that MTY1's B shift ends at midnight, or
what the weather was on the day a site fell behind. Before measuring performance, build the reference data that
makes measurement fair.

**Sources**
- **Warehouse master**: an Excel workbook in `landing/files/facilities/` maintained by Ops (capacity, dock doors,
  pallet positions, pick faces, shifts, cutoffs). New versions appear when something changes, and people edit it
  by hand.
- **Public holidays**: the Nager.Date API for the US, Canada and Mexico.
- **Weather**: the Open-Meteo historical and forecast APIs, for each site's coordinates.
- **Business-day calendar**: per warehouse, built from all of the above.

**Talk to:** Shanice Carter (how shifts and cutoffs really work on the floor), Marcus Bell (WMS time conventions),
Luis Moreno (which holidays actually close a building).

**Where to start:** **Source systems → Business files** and **Public APIs** describe both kinds of source, with example URLs. The tasks
are in order, smallest first, so take P2.S1.T2 next. Luis Moreno owns the warehouse master.

**Definition of Done**
- All sub-tasks done; reference tables in silver with tests and a documented refresh cadence
- Calendar checked against at least one GM's description of their shifts
- Each sub-task merged through its own PR (branch `feat/DATA-<n>-…`, Conventional Commits with the key, self-review, CI green)
acceptance_criteria: Every warehouse-master workbook version ingested with effective dates; layout changes never silently mis-map
Public holidays for the US, Canada and Mexico for the full history plus the next 12 months, mapped to sites
Daily weather per warehouse for the full history, kept current
Business-day calendar per warehouse with local date, working-day flag, shifts, cutoffs and peak-season flag
Reference data has DQ checks (completeness, gaps, duplicates) in the P1 results table

rewrite history: last year's utilization uses last year's capacity.

Work in this order: load every file as it is, with its name, timestamp and checksum. Then build a silver table with
effective dates, one row per site per version. Then make the load refuse a file whose headers aren't what you expect.

**Where to start:** Open the newest `warehouse_master_<yyyymmdd>.xlsx`, sheets `Sites` and `Zones`; **Source systems → Business files**
has a diagram of every column. Compare `Site Code`, `Site Name` and `Time Zone` with `wms.warehouse`
(`warehouse_code`, `warehouse_name`, `time_zone`). Luis Moreno owns the workbook.
acceptance_criteria: Every workbook version loaded with file name, file timestamp and checksum

**Sponsor:** Luis Moreno (VP Operations). **Infrastructure owner:** Kevin O'Hara (IT Infrastructure).

> "By the time the morning scorecard tells me ATL1 missed cutoff yesterday, the trucks are long gone. I want to see
> it at 2 pm, not tomorrow at 8." (Luis)

Everything you've built so far runs on batch pulls from the WMS, and the WMS is unfriendly to batch. It physically
deletes rows: cancelled order lines, inventory at zero quantity, voided labels, and old tasks. `order_line` has no
change timestamp at all. Even an hourly pull would be wrong. The Postgres server already runs with logical replication
on, publications exist for each source schema, and your `etl_reader` login has the REPLICATION attribute. Kevin owns
the server and its disk.

**What this project delivers**
- An architecture decision (ADR) for change data capture that Kevin and Sam Okafor sign off.
- A CDC pipeline for the WMS that handles inserts, updates and hard deletes, is ordered and replayable, and is safe for the server.
- Streaming models for live order status, backlog, throughput and current inventory.
- Exactly-once behaviour you can prove, plus backfill and replay procedures.
- Alerting and SLAs: freshness ≤ 5 minutes, and replication slot health.
- Dashboard **P6-D1 Live Operations Board**, shown on the shipping-office TVs and on Luis's phone.

**Success measures**
- Board data ≤ 5 minutes behind the WMS (P95) during site operating hours.
- Zero lost, duplicated or "zombie" rows after restarts, replays and WMS releases, proven by daily reconciliation.
- A stopped consumer can never fill the server's disk without hours of warning.
- Kevin is comfortable owning the runbooks on a weekend.

**Constraints**
- The source runs in Docker on your laptop, and nothing in the cloud can connect to it. Kevin and Mei will not approve exposing Postgres to the internet.
- Free tier: Databricks Free Edition is serverless only, with one 2X-Small SQL warehouse, one active pipeline per pipeline
  type and 5 concurrent job tasks. Snowflake trial credits run out. An always-on 24/7 design may be unaffordable or not
  allowed, and the ADR must say how you'll live with that.

epic.summary: Cold Chain & Lot Traceability: prove every lot stayed in range, and find it fast when it didn't
epic.description:
**Sponsor:** Dr. Ayesha Khan (Quality & Food Safety Manager). **Sensors and controls:** Grace Liu (Facilities & Controls).

> "When an auditor asks me to prove a lot of yogurt stayed between 2 and 8 degrees from receipt to shipment, I print
> charts from three systems and staple them together. When a client recalls a lot, it takes us two days to tell them
> where it went. The food traceability rule expects records within 24 hours." (Ayesha)

CHI1 is the cold-chain building, with cooler and freezer zones, and TOR1 has a cooler. The other sites are ambient
but still monitored. Sensors report about every 5 minutes through gateways. The gateways buffer when the network
drops and flush late, and device clocks drift. The WMS tracks lots on receipts, inventory and the inventory ledger.
After an excursion, Quality puts the exposed lots on HOLD and later releases or destroys them.

**What this project delivers**
- Reliable telemetry ingestion that copes with late flushes, duplicates and clock drift.
- Excursion detection to Quality's SOP, with exposure per lot and a hold compliance check.
- Lot genealogy from receipt through inventory and the ledger to shipment.
- A recall trace that lists every order, consignee and carrier for a lot, within hours.
- Sensor health: stuck readings, spikes, dropouts, battery and calibration.
- Dashboards **P7-D1 Cold Chain Monitor** and **P7-D2 Recall Trace**.

**Success measures**
- Every regulated zone's time in range is known, and a broken sensor shows as "unknown", never as "in range".
- A mock recall drill produces a complete, reconciled recall package in under 2 hours.
- Ayesha uses the monitor in her weekly Quality review instead of stapled printouts.

**Talk to:** Ayesha (SOP, thresholds, holds, recalls), Grace (sensors, gateways, calibration), Marcus Bell (where lots
live in the WMS), Omar Haddad (client communication during a recall), Mei Tanaka (consignee PII in recall packages).

> sometimes twice. And a couple of devices think it's a different time than it is." (Grace)

**Source:** the `iot` database, schema `telemetry`.
- `sensor` is the sensor master.
- `sensor_reading` has `device_ts_ms`: epoch milliseconds from the device clock, UTC, which can drift. Its
  `ingested_at` is when the gateway landed the row.
- `dock_door_event` holds door OPEN and CLOSE events.

Large. `sensor` rows are updated when a probe is recalibrated. A publication
`hl_iot_cdc` exists if you want to use it.

**What good looks like**
- Every reading lands exactly once, even when it arrives hours late.
- Device time is converted correctly, and clock drift is detected rather than trusted.
- A regular 5-minute grid per sensor with explicit gaps. Raw readings are kept for audit.

This is the capstone. It opens by finding out what the platform you've built costs and where it's slow, before
anything new lands on it. Then comes governance: classification, masking, roles and audit. Then per-client row-level
security for a client-facing portal, and a data share for clients who want raw data. The executive scorecard reuses
the semantic layer. It finishes with a final executive readout and a portfolio package.

**How this project runs:** the tickets here say what the business needs and who decides what. The method, and the
case for it, are yours. Expect your stakeholders to disagree with each other.

**What this project delivers**
- A performance and cost review of projects 1 to 7, with P8's own dashboards held to the same target when they ship.
- Governance as code: PII classification, masking of consignee name, address, phone and email, role-based access, and audit.
- Row-level security per client for a portal, proven by negative tests.
- A data share, or a governed extract, for a pilot client.
- An executive scorecard model reusing the metric catalog, tied out to Finance and Operations.
- Dashboards **P8-D1 Client Portal** and **P8-D2 Executive Scorecard**, plus the final executive readout.

**Success measures**
- Zero cross-client leaks in the negative test suite, and Mei's sign-off.
- Every scorecard KPI has an owner and ties out to its source dashboard.
- Platform cost per month known, with the top 3 savings implemented.
- A portfolio-ready package: architecture diagram, demo video, write-up.

**Constraints:** what free tiers allow for users, groups, sharing and audit logs varies by edition and changes over
time. Check the current documentation for your tier, use what's there, and write down what you emulated and what
production would need instead.
